VO.q: The patient had two episodes of emesis after surgery and was given ice chips instead of a meal. As used in this sentence, what does the word "emesis" mean?
VO.w: Emesis is vomiting (or the vomited material).

n.0: Dizziness can follow surgery, but emesis means vomiting.
n.1: Bed-wetting is enuresis, a look-alike word.
n.3: Fainting is syncope.

VO.q: A runner who collapsed near the finish line was treated in the medical tent for hyperthermia. Based on its word parts, what does hyperthermia mean?
VO.w: hyper- means above or excessive and therm means heat, so hyperthermia is an abnormally high body temperature.

n.0: Abnormally low body heat is hypothermia; hypo- means below.
n.1: Loss of body water is dehydration (hydr = water); the root here is therm (heat).
n.3: Excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis) shares the prefix hyper-, but the root therm means heat, not sweat.

VO.q: The nurse documented objective data, such as heart rate and wound size, in the chart. What is the best definition of the word "objective" in this sentence?
VO.w: Objective means based on observable facts and measurements.

n.0: Information from the patient's own report is subjective, the opposite.
n.1: Likely to offend is objectionable, a look-alike.
n.2: Detail fits charting loosely, but objective refers to the source of the data.

VO.q: The patient pointed to her epigastric area when she described a burning pain after large meals. Based on its prefix, where is this area?
VO.w: epi- means upon or over and gastr/o means stomach, so the epigastric area lies over the stomach (the upper middle abdomen).

n.1: Behind is retro-, as in retroperitoneal.
n.2: Within is endo- or intra-; epi- means upon or over.
n.3: Below is hypo- or sub- (the hypogastric area lies below the stomach).

VO.q: Long-term smoking has deleterious effects on nearly every organ in the body. What is the best definition of the word "deleterious" in this sentence?
VO.w: Deleterious means harmful or damaging.

n.0: Deliberate means intended, a look-alike.
n.1: Uncertain effects would be unclear ones; deleterious effects are harmful.
n.2: Delayed fits the phrase long-term loosely, but deleterious means harmful.

VO.q: Because her asthma is chronic, Lena keeps an inhaler in her backpack all year. As used in this sentence, what does the word "chronic" mean?
VO.w: Chronic means lasting a long time or recurring often.

n.1: That is chronological, a look-alike word built on the same root.
n.2: That is acute, the opposite.
n.3: That is critical; chronic describes duration, not danger.

VO.q: During chemotherapy, a patient's blood test revealed leukopenia, so the nurse reviewed infection precautions with him. Based on its word parts, what does leukopenia mean?
o: A deficiency of white blood cells
A cancer of the white blood cells
An excess of white blood cells
A deficiency of red blood cells
VO.w: leuk/o means white and -penia means deficiency, so leukopenia is a shortage of white blood cells (which explains the infection precautions).

n.1: Cancer would be shown by carcin/o or -oma (or -emia in leukemia, a blood condition); -penia means deficiency.
n.2: An excess would use hyper- or -cytosis; -penia means deficiency.
n.3: Red is erythr/o; leuk/o means white.

VO.q: The therapist asked Mr. Chen to abduct his arm until it was level with his shoulder. What is the best definition of the word "abduct" in this sentence?
o: move it away from the midline
turn it around its long axis
VO.w: Abduct means to move a limb away from the midline (ab- = away from).

n.0: Bending a joint is flexion.
n.2: Turning around an axis is rotation.
n.3: Toward the midline is adduct, the opposite (ad- = toward).

VO.q: The care team respected the patient's autonomy when she declined further dialysis. What is the best definition of the word "autonomy" in this sentence?
VO.w: Autonomy is the right or ability to make one's own decisions (auto- = self, nom = law).

n.1: The family's wishes are not her own decision; autonomy is personal.
n.2: Beliefs may shape a choice, but autonomy is the right to make it.
n.3: Privacy is confidentiality; autonomy is self-determination.

VO.q: Which word means "toward the midline of the body"?
VO.w: Medial means toward the midline; the inner ankle is on the medial side of the leg.

n.0: Dorsal refers to the back side of the body.
n.1: Lateral means away from the midline, the opposite.
n.2: Proximal means nearer the trunk or point of attachment, not the midline.

VO.q: Whenever Ana rolled over in bed, her vertigo returned and she gripped the mattress until it passed. What is the best definition of the word "vertigo" in this sentence?
VO.w: Vertigo is the sensation that oneself or the surroundings are spinning.

n.0: Fainting is syncope, the classic partner trap.
n.2: A racing heartbeat is a palpitation.
n.3: Nausea often comes with vertigo, but it is a stomach feeling, not spinning.

VO.q: Before the clinical trial began, researchers sorted the volunteers into groups so that each group was homogeneous in age. Based on its prefix, what does homogeneous mean here?
VO.w: homo-/homeo- means same or similar, so a group homogeneous in age is made of people of similar ages.

n.0: Different is hetero- (heterogeneous), the opposite prefix.
n.1: Many is multi- or poly-, not homo-.
n.2: Half is hemi- or semi-, not homo-.

VO.q: After the patient's hip surgery, the doctor prescribed an anticoagulant to take for several weeks. Based on the prefix, what does an anticoagulant do?
VO.w: anti- means against, and coagulant refers to clotting, so an anticoagulant works against the clotting of blood.

n.0: anti- does mean against, but the root coagul refers to clotting, not infection (an anti-infective works against infection).
n.1: Speeding up clotting is the opposite of anti- (against).
n.3: Breaking down would be shown by -lysis (as in thrombolysis), not by anti-.

VO.q: Patients must abstain from food and drink for eight hours before the procedure. What is the best definition of the word "abstain" in this sentence?
VO.w: Abstain means to choose not to do or have something: the patient has nothing to eat or drink.

n.0: Asking about food is not the meaning of abstain.
n.2: Tracking intake fits the sentence loosely, but abstain means not to have it.
n.3: Cutting down still allows some food and drink; abstain means to go without it entirely for that time.

VO.q: During the resident's quarterly medication review, the geriatric care team flagged polypharmacy as a risk for falls. Based on its word parts, what is polypharmacy?
o: Use of several pharmacies to fill orders
Use of a drug that affects many organs
Use of many medications at the same time
Use of one medication at too high a dose
VO.w: poly- means many and pharmac/o refers to drugs, so polypharmacy is the use of many medications at the same time, which raises the risk of side effects, drug interactions and falls in older adults.

n.0: Here pharmacy refers to drugs (pharmac/o), not to the stores that fill prescriptions; polypharmacy is about how many medications a person takes.
n.1: poly- (many) applies to the drugs themselves; nothing in the word refers to organs or body systems.
n.3: poly- means many, so the word refers to the number of drugs, not to one drug at too high a dose (one is mono- or uni-).

VO.q: The hospital funded a retrospective study of screening outcomes at its three community clinics. Based on its word parts, what does retrospective mean?
VO.w: retro- means backward and spect means look, so retrospective means looking back at past events.

n.0: Within is intra- or endo-, not retro-.
n.2: Looking ahead is the meaning of pro- or pre- words such as prospective; retro- means backward.
n.3: Across is trans-, not retro-.

VO.q: Which word means "to chew"?
VO.w: Masticate means to chew; mastication is the first step of digestion.

n.0: Macerate means to soften by soaking.
n.1: Regurgitate means to bring swallowed food back up.
n.2: Ingest means to take in by swallowing.

VO.q: The bruise was on the lateral side of Ms. Brooks's right thigh. What is the best definition of the word "lateral" in this sentence?
o: toward the back of the body
toward the front of the body
VO.w: Lateral means toward the side, away from the midline of the body: the outer side of the thigh.

n.0: Toward the back is posterior.
n.1: Toward the front is anterior.
n.3: Toward the midline is medial, the opposite.

VO.q: A patient with repeated attacks of pain from gallstones is scheduled for a cholecystectomy next week. Using all of its word parts, what will the surgeon do?
VO.w: Step 1: chol/e means bile and cyst/o means bladder or sac, so cholecyst is the bile sac (gallbladder). Step 2: -ectomy means surgical removal. A cholecystectomy removes the gallbladder.

n.0: Visual examination is -scopy, not -ectomy.
n.2: cyst/o alone can mean the urinary bladder, but chol/e (bile) makes this the gallbladder.
n.3: Cutting into an organ is -otomy, not -ectomy.

VO.q: The nurse recorded a baseline blood pressure when Mr. Shah arrived on the unit. What is the best definition of the word "baseline" in this sentence?
o: an ideal value for good health
a target value set by the doctor
VO.w: A baseline is a first measurement used for later comparison.

n.0: A baseline can be any value; it is defined by timing, not by being low.
n.1: An ideal standard is a benchmark, a look-alike idea.
n.2: A target is a goal; a baseline is the starting point.

VO.q: The infection had become systemic, and Mr. Ng was started on intravenous antibiotics. What is the best definition of the word "systemic" in this sentence?
VO.w: Systemic means affecting the whole body rather than one part.

n.0: Applied to the skin is topical.
n.1: Orderly and methodical is systematic, a look-alike.
n.3: Limited to one area is localized, the opposite.

VO.q: After exposure to the virus on the cruise, healthy passengers were placed in quarantine for two weeks. What is the best definition of the word "quarantine" in this sentence?
VO.w: Quarantine separates people who were exposed to a disease, but are not sick, to see whether they become ill.

n.0: Vaccines prevent disease; quarantine is separation.
n.1: Separating people who are already sick is isolation; these passengers are healthy.
n.2: A dispute is a quarrel, a look-alike word.

VO.q: A community clinic posts a flyer for free antenatal classes on Tuesday evenings. Based on its prefix, when are the classes meant to help parents?
VO.w: ante- means before and natal refers to birth, so antenatal classes are for the period before the baby is born (the same meaning as prenatal).

n.1: ante- means before, not during; during would use intra-.
n.2: After birth would be postnatal; post- means after.
n.3: The newborn period is neonatal (neo- = new), not antenatal.

VO.q: After a stroke, a patient with hemiplegia began working with a physical therapist three times a week. Based on its word parts, what does hemiplegia mean?
o: Paralysis affecting both of the legs
Paralysis on one side of the body
Paralysis of all four of the limbs
Paralysis caused by a brain bleed
VO.w: hemi- means half and -plegia means paralysis, so hemiplegia is paralysis of one half (one side) of the body.

n.0: Paralysis of both legs is paraplegia; hemi- refers to one side, not both legs.
n.2: Paralysis of all four limbs is quadriplegia; quadri- means four.
n.3: hemi- (half) is not hem/o (blood); the word says nothing about bleeding.

VO.q: Jordan felt well for a month, but a relapse sent him back to the clinic in March. What is the best definition of the word "relapse" in this sentence?
VO.w: A relapse is a return of illness after a period of improvement.

n.0: A decrease in symptoms is remission.
n.2: Collapse is a sound-alike; relapse is the illness returning, not a fall.
n.3: A full recovery is the opposite of a relapse.

VO.q: Before inserting the urinary catheter, the nurse used aseptic technique and a new pair of gloves. As used in this sentence, what does the word "aseptic" mean?
VO.w: Aseptic means free of disease-causing microorganisms.

n.1: Able to kill germs is antiseptic, an agent rather than a germ-free state.
n.2: Infected is septic; the a- prefix means without.
n.3: Careful practice fits the sentence loosely, but aseptic means germ-free.

VO.q: The eye doctor used drops to dilate Maria's pupils before the retinal exam. What is the best definition of the word "dilate" in this sentence?
VO.w: Dilate means to widen or enlarge an opening or vessel.

n.0: Weakening with liquid is dilute, the dilate sound-alike.
n.2: Moistening fits eye drops loosely, but dilate means to widen.
n.3: Narrowing is constrict, the opposite.

VO.q: Mr. Ito was reluctant to use the walker, worried that others would see him as frail. What is the best definition of the word "reluctant" in this sentence?
VO.w: Reluctant means unwilling and hesitant.

n.0: Worry about looking frail explains why he hesitated, but reluctant means unwilling, not embarrassed.
n.2: Eager is the opposite of reluctant.
n.3: He is able to use it; reluctant describes his unwillingness.

VO.q: After her appendectomy, Ms. Rivera spent two weeks of convalescence at her sister's home. What is the best definition of the word "convalescence" in this sentence?
VO.w: Convalescence is the period of gradual recovery after an illness or operation.

n.0: Restoring ability through therapy is rehabilitation, a related but different word.
n.1: Separation fits a stay away from home loosely, but that is isolation.
n.3: This confuses convalescence with convulsion, a look-alike word.

VO.q: By evening the patient was agitated, pacing the room and tugging at her blanket. What is the best definition of the word "agitated" in this sentence?
VO.w: Agitated means troubled, nervous and restless, as shown by pacing and tugging.

n.0: Pain could cause pacing, but agitated names a nervous, restless state of mind, not pain.
n.1: Drowsy and sluggish is lethargic, the opposite state.
n.3: Not knowing time and place is disorientation, a different sign.

VO.q: Climbing one flight of stairs now brings on dyspnea, so Mrs. Owens stops on the landing to rest. What is the best definition of the word "dyspnea" in this sentence?
VO.w: Dyspnea is difficult or labored breathing: dys- (difficult) + -pnea (breathing).

n.0: Difficult swallowing is dysphagia (-phagia = eating, swallowing).
n.1: Painful urination is dysuria (-uria = urine).
n.2: Difficult speech is dysphasia (-phasia = speech).

VO.q: Before discharge, the nurse reviewed the postoperative care instructions with the patient's family. Based on the prefix, when are these instructions meant to be followed?
VO.w: post- means after, so postoperative care is the care given after an operation.

n.0: Before surgery is preoperative; pre- means before.
n.1: Between is the meaning of inter-, not post-.
n.2: During surgery is intraoperative; intra- means within.

VO.q: A warning label on a can of cleaning solvent reads, "Inflammable: store away from heat, sparks, and open flames." Based on the context, what does inflammable mean?
VO.w: Here in- does not mean not: inflammable means the same as flammable. The context (keep it away from heat, sparks and flames) confirms that the product catches fire easily.

n.0: This also reads in- as "not," which contradicts the instruction to store it away from heat.
n.1: This reads in- as "not," but the warning to keep the can away from flames shows it can catch fire.
n.2: The label's warning is about fire, and nothing in the word parts refers to breathing.

VO.q: The biopsy showed the lump was benign, and Ms. Clark cried with relief in the exam room. What is the best definition of the word "benign" in this sentence?
VO.w: Benign means not harmful; in medicine, not cancerous.

n.0: Likely to spread describes malignant, the opposite.
n.1: A fluid-filled lump is a cyst; benign describes harm, not contents.
n.3: A small lump would also bring relief, but benign describes whether a growth is harmful or cancerous, not its size.

VO.q: The pharmacist warned that the new pain reliever is far more potent than the old one. What is the best definition of the word "potent" in this sentence?
VO.w: Potent means powerful or strong in effect: a small dose of a potent drug acts strongly.

n.0: Present but inactive is latent.
n.1: This confuses potent with potential.
n.3: Open and unblocked is patent, a look-alike word.

VO.q: Touching the inside of the cap can contaminate the vial, so the nurse handles it by the edges. As used in this sentence, what does the word "contaminate" mean?
VO.w: Contaminate means to make impure or unclean, especially by introducing germs.

n.0: Making stronger is concentrate, a look-alike.
n.1: Thinking about is contemplate, a sound-alike.
n.3: Making germ-free is decontaminate or sterilize, the opposite.

VO.q: The nurse charted bradycardia after counting the patient's pulse at the start of morning rounds. Based on its prefix, what does bradycardia mean?
VO.w: brady- means slow and cardi/o means heart, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate.

n.1: Neither brady- nor cardia refers to rhythm; an irregular rhythm is an arrhythmia.
n.2: A fast heart rate is tachycardia; tachy- means fast, the opposite of brady-.
n.3: Pain would come from a suffix such as -algia or -dynia; brady- describes speed, not pain.

VO.q: The lab identified the pathogen responsible for the outbreak at the day care center. As used in this sentence, what does the word "pathogen" mean?
VO.w: A pathogen is a microorganism or agent that causes disease (path- = disease, -gen = producer).

n.0: A protective protein made by the body is an antibody.
n.2: A substance that triggers an immune response is an antigen.
n.3: A specialist who studies disease is a pathologist.

VO.q: The physician told the unit clerk that she would dictate her notes on each patient after morning rounds. Based on its root, what will the physician do with her notes?
o: Send them on to another office
VO.w: The root dict means say, so to dictate is to say words aloud for someone (or a device) to record.

n.0: Looking is the meaning of spec/spect (as in inspect).
n.2: Sending is the meaning of mit/mis (as in transmit).
n.3: Writing is the meaning of scrib/script (as in prescription).

VO.q: The teenager seemed indifferent to the nurse's warnings about vaping and kept scrolling on his phone. What is the best definition of the word indifferent in this sentence?
VO.w: Indifferent means having no particular interest or concern.

n.1: Hostility would show anger; scrolling on his phone shows lack of interest, not aggression.
n.2: Fear is the reaction the warnings aimed for; indifferent is the lack of any reaction.
n.3: Confusion is a topic fit for a warning, but indifferent means not caring.

VO.q: Which word means "surgical removal of tissue"?
VO.w: Excision is surgical removal (ex- = out, cis = cut). Compare incision, a cut into tissue.

n.1: Exclusion means leaving something out; it only looks like excision.
n.2: A suture is a stitch that closes a wound.
n.3: An incision is a cut made into tissue; excision cuts tissue out.

VO.q: Health officials warned that the new strain of influenza was more virulent than last year's. What is the best definition of the word "virulent" in this sentence?
VO.w: In a medical sentence, virulent means highly harmful and able to cause severe disease.

n.0: Vaccine resistance fits a new strain loosely, but it is not virulence.
n.2: Duration fits a new strain loosely, but virulent describes how severe and harmful the disease is, not how long it lasts.
n.3: Caused by a virus is viral, a look-alike word.

VO.q: Before the rash appeared, Mr. Lee reported a general malaise that had lasted about a week. As used in this sentence, what does the word "malaise" mean?
VO.w: Malaise is a vague, general feeling of being unwell or uncomfortable.

n.0: An urge to vomit is nausea, a more specific stomach sensation.
n.1: Ill will is malice, a sound-alike.
n.2: That is malady, a look-alike word. Malaise is a feeling, not a named disease.

VO.q: Climbing six flights of stairs after knee surgery was an arduous task for Mr. Brooks. Which word means the opposite of arduous as used in this sentence?
VO.w: Arduous means very difficult and tiring, so its opposite is effortless.

n.0: Exhausting is close to a synonym of arduous, not its opposite.
n.2: Lengthy describes duration; it is not the opposite of hard and tiring.
n.3: Climbing after surgery may be risky, but dangerous is a topic fit, not the opposite of difficult.

VO.q: After the test, the technician handed the cardiologist a printed tracing that recorded the electrical activity of the patient's heart. Based on its suffix, what is this printed tracing called?
VO.w: Step 1: the item is the record itself, not the process or the machine. Step 2: -gram means a record, so the printed tracing is an electrocardiogram.

n.0: -graph names the instrument that does the recording, not its output.
n.1: -graphy names the process of recording, not the printed record.
n.2: -logy means the study of, a field of knowledge, not a record.

VO.q: After the patient's femur fracture, the orthopedic team placed his leg in traction until surgery could be scheduled. Based on its root, what does traction apply to the leg?
o: A twisting force that turns the limb
A steady pulling force on the limb
A brace that carries the limb's weight
A cut that opens the limb's tissue
VO.w: The root tract means pull, so traction is a steady pulling force (used to align a broken bone).

n.0: Turning is the meaning of vert/vers, not tract.
n.2: Carrying is the meaning of port, not tract.
n.3: Cutting is the meaning of sect (as in dissect), not tract.

VO.q: The patient's abrupt change in behavior after the fall prompted the nurse to call the physician. As used in this sentence, what does the word "abrupt" mean?
VO.w: Abrupt means sudden and unexpected.

n.0: Repeated describes a recurring pattern, not a sudden one.
n.1: Slow and gradual is the opposite of abrupt.
n.2: Minor and brief describes size and length, not suddenness.

VO.q: The patient described a sharp intercostal pain that worsened each time she took a deep breath. Based on its prefix, where is the pain?
VO.w: inter- means between and cost/o means rib, so intercostal pain is felt between the ribs.

n.0: Around is peri- or circum-, not inter-.
n.1: Below the ribs is subcostal (sub- = under).
n.3: Within is intra-, the look-alike prefix; inter- means between.

VO.q: Because she had chickenpox as a child, Tasha is immune to the disease. As used in this sentence, what does the word "immune" mean?
VO.w: Immune means protected against a particular disease.

n.0: A carrier harbors and spreads a pathogen; immune means protected.
n.1: An allergy is an overreaction to a substance, not protection.
n.3: Easily infected means susceptible, the opposite.

VO.q: The dermatologist measured a small lesion on Carlos's forearm and scheduled a follow-up visit. What is the best definition of the word "lesion" in this sentence?
VO.w: A lesion is an area of abnormal or damaged tissue, such as a sore, wound or growth.

n.1: Lotion is a sound-alike; a lesion is the tissue being examined, not a treatment.
n.2: A vein can be seen on a forearm, but it is normal anatomy, not a lesion.
n.3: Numbness is a change in sensation; a lesion is an area of abnormal or damaged tissue that can be seen and measured.

VO.q: The pancreas secretes insulin directly into the bloodstream. What is the best definition of the word "secrete" in this sentence?
VO.w: Secrete means to produce and release a substance; glands secrete hormones such as insulin.

n.0: Breaking down is metabolize.
n.1: Storing keeps a substance; secretes means releasing it.
n.3: Eliminating waste is excrete.

VO.q: To track her new walking program, an adult patient agreed to wear a pedometer on her waistband all week. Based on its word parts and the context, what does a pedometer most likely measure?
VO.w: ped can mean foot or child, and the context (an adult's walking program) points to foot. A -meter measures, so a pedometer counts steps taken on foot.

n.1: Heart rate would involve cardi/o (heart), which is not in the word.
n.2: Body heat would involve therm (heat), as in thermometer.
n.3: ped can mean child, but the patient is an adult tracking her walking, so foot is the meaning here.

VO.q: The team shifted to palliative care when Mr. Alvarez's cancer stopped responding to chemotherapy. What is the best definition of the word "palliative" in this sentence?
VO.w: Palliative means relieving symptoms such as pain without curing the disease, which fits a patient whose cancer no longer responds to treatment.

n.0: That is curative care; palliative care relieves symptoms when a cure is not the goal.
n.1: Preventing disease is prophylactic, the classic palliative look-alike in care words.
n.3: This fits the setting loosely, but palliative describes the purpose of care, not its location.

VO.q: Pediatric cardiologists often treat congenital heart defects in infants and young children. What is the best definition of the word "congenital" in this sentence?
VO.w: Congenital means present at birth. Not every congenital condition is inherited.

n.1: Inherited is hereditary; a congenital condition may or may not be inherited.
n.2: A condition that develops later in life is acquired, the opposite.
n.3: Pleasant and friendly is congenial, a sound-alike.

VO.q: To check for trapped fluid, Dr. Grant will percuss the patient's back over each lung. As used in this sentence, what does the word "percuss" mean?
VO.w: Percuss means to tap a body surface to judge what lies beneath by the sound produced.

n.0: Persuade is a sound-alike with no exam meaning.
n.2: Pressing with the hands is palpate.
n.3: Listening through a stethoscope is auscultate.

MA.q: A unit has 12 RNs and 20 nursing assistants. How many RNs must be added so that the ratio of RNs to nursing assistants becomes 4:5?
MA.w: With 20 nursing assistants, 5 parts = 20, so one part = 4. RNs needed: 4 × 4 = 16. RNs to add: 16 - 12 = 4.

n.0: This is the number of RNs needed in total, not the number to add.
n.2: This compares ratio terms: 12:20 is 3:5, and 4 - 3 = 1. Each part stands for 4 people, not 1.
n.3: This reverses the ratio, making RNs 5/4 of 20 (25), then subtracts 12.

MA.q: A patient-education poster is enlarged proportionally from a draft that is 8 inches wide and 10 inches tall. The poster is 26 inches wide. How tall is the poster? Enter the number of inches.

tr.28: Added the 18-inch increase in width to the height instead of scaling.
tr.20.8: Set up the ratio upside down (26 × 8 ÷ 10).

MA.w: Set up width/height: 8/10 = 26/h. Cross-multiply: 8h = 260, so h = 32.5 inches.

MA.q: Solve for x: x/6 + 4 = 11.
MA.w: Subtract 4 from both sides: x/6 = 7. Multiply both sides by 6: x = 42. Check: 42/6 + 4 = 7 + 4 = 11.

n.0: Sign error: 4 was added to 11 instead of subtracted, giving x/6 = 15.
n.1: This divides by 6 instead of multiplying. To undo x/6, multiply both sides by 6.
n.3: This multiplies 11 by 6 but not the 4. Multiplying every term by 6 gives x + 24 = 66, so x = 42.

MA.q: Write 160% as a mixed number in lowest terms.

n.1: 1 6/10 has the right value, but 6 and 10 still share a factor of 2, so it is not in lowest terms.
n.2: 3/5 is 60%; it drops the 100% that makes up the whole 1.

MA.q: To estimate 6.8 × 4.6, a student rounds both numbers to the nearest whole number and calculates 7 × 5 = 35. How does this estimate compare with the exact product?
o: An exact estimate, because the rounding errors are both less than 0.5
An underestimate, because 4.6 was rounded more than 6.8
An overestimate by 0.6, the total amount the factors were rounded up
An overestimate, because both factors were rounded up
MA.w: Both factors were rounded up (6.8 → 7 and 4.6 → 5), so the estimate is too high. Exact: 6.8 × 4.6 = 31.28, so 35 is 3.72 too high.

n.0: The rounding errors are small, but they still change the product (35 vs 31.28).
n.1: Rounding both factors up makes the product larger, so the estimate is too high, not too low.
n.2: The round-offs are multiplied by the other factors, so the error is 35 - 31.28 = 3.72, not 0.6.

MA.q: A provider orders heparin 7,500 units. The vial is labeled 5,000 units per mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Enter the number of milliliters.
MA.w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 7,500 ÷ 5,000 × 1 mL = 1.5 mL. As a proportion: 5,000 units/1 mL = 7,500 units/x, so x = 1.5 mL.

MA.q: What is √0.81?

n.0: 0.405 is 0.81 ÷ 2; a square root is not half the number.
n.1: 0.09 × 0.09 = 0.0081, not 0.81; the decimal places were miscounted.
n.2: 0.6561 is 0.81², the square, not the square root.

MA.q: This fall a pharmacy gave 135% of the number of flu vaccines it gave last fall. Last fall it gave 1,200 vaccines. How many flu vaccines did it give this fall?

n.0: This is 35% of 1,200, the increase alone, not 135% of 1,200.
n.3: This adds 135% of 1,200 to the original 1,200, counting last fall's vaccines twice.

MA.q: Gym A charges a $30 joining fee plus $25 per month. Gym B charges a $90 joining fee plus $19 per month. For the number of months at which the total costs of the two gyms are equal, what is that total cost?
MA.w: Set the totals equal: 30 + 25m = 90 + 19m. Subtract 19m and 30 from both sides: 6m = 60, so m = 10 months. Total: 30 + 25(10) = $280. Check Gym B: 90 + 19(10) = $280.

n.0: This is Gym A's monthly charges for 10 months without the $30 joining fee.
n.1: This mixes the plans: Gym B's $90 fee with Gym A's $25 monthly rate for 10 months.
n.2: This adds the fees instead of subtracting them, giving 6m = 120 and m = 20 months, then 30 + 25(20) = $530.

MA.q: A pharmacy packs 1,000 tablets into bottles of 30. How many bottles can be filled, and how many tablets are left over?
MA.w: 1,000 ÷ 30 = 33 R 10, because 30 × 33 = 990 and 1,000 - 990 = 10. So 33 full bottles with 10 tablets left over.

n.1: A remainder of 40 is larger than 30, so another bottle can still be filled.
n.2: 3 left over reads the decimal 33.33 as a remainder of 3; the remainder is 1,000 - 990 = 10 tablets.
n.3: 34 bottles would need 34 × 30 = 1,020 tablets, more than the 1,000 on hand.

MA.w: Subtract 0.25x from both sides: 3.5 = 0.5x - 1.5. Add 1.5: 5 = 0.5x. Divide by 0.5: x = 10. Check: 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 and 7.5 - 1.5 = 6.

n.1: This adds 0.25x to 0.75x instead of subtracting it, leaving 1x = 5.
n.2: This multiplies 5 by 0.5 instead of dividing 5 by 0.5.
n.3: Sign error when moving -1.5: adding 1.5 to both sides gives 3.5 + 1.5 = 5, not 3.5 - 1.5 = 2.

MA.q: Which list orders these times from earliest to latest in one day: 0915, 1:30 p.m., 1105, 12:45 a.m.?

n.0: This puts 12:45 a.m. at the end of the day; it is 0045, 45 minutes after midnight.
n.1: This treats 12:45 a.m. as 12:45 p.m. (1245), which would fall after 1105.
n.3: This reads 1:30 p.m. as 0130 and 12:45 a.m. as the end of the day.

MA.q: At lunch a patient is served a 480 mL nutritional shake and a 240 mL cup of juice. She drinks 300 mL of the shake and all of the juice. What percent of the total fluid served did she drink?
MA.w: Total served: 480 + 240 = 720 mL. Total drunk: 300 + 240 = 540 mL. Percent = part ÷ whole × 100 = 540 ÷ 720 × 100 = 75%.

n.1: This is the shake alone, 300 ÷ 480. The juice she drank and the juice served both belong in the totals.
n.2: This is the percent of the fluid she left (180 ÷ 720), not the percent she drank.
n.3: This averages the two percents (62.5% and 100%). The containers hold different amounts, so combine the milliliters first: 540 ÷ 720.

MA.q: A child who weighs 22 lb is prescribed 25 mg per kg. The liquid contains 125 mg per 5 mL. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milliliters should be given?

n.0: This uses 22 lb as kilograms: 25 × 22 = 550 mg, then 550 ÷ 125 × 5 = 22 mL.
n.1: This stops at desired ÷ have (250 ÷ 125 = 2) and does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.
n.3: This multiplies 22 by 2.2 instead of dividing, giving 48.4 kg and 48.4 mL.

MA.q: An order is for 250 mg every 8 hours. Capsules contain 125 mg each. How many capsules are needed for 3 days?
MA.w: Per dose: 250 ÷ 125 = 2 capsules. Doses per day: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. Per day: 2 × 3 = 6 capsules. For 3 days: 6 × 3 = 18 capsules.

n.0: This is the number of capsules for 1 day, not 3 days.
n.1: This counts 4 doses a day. Every 8 hours gives 24 ÷ 8 = 3 doses a day.
n.3: This is the number of doses in 3 days; each dose is 2 capsules.

MA.q: A roll of medical tape held 6 1/4 yards. A nurse used 2 3/4 yards while dressing wounds during a shift. How many yards of tape are left on the roll?
MA.w: 1/4 is less than 3/4, so borrow 1 from 6: 6 1/4 = 5 5/4. Then 5 5/4 - 2 3/4 = 3 2/4 = 3 1/2 yards.

n.0: 4 1/2 subtracts 1/4 from 3/4 instead of borrowing (6 - 2 = 4 and 3/4 - 1/4 = 1/2).
n.1: 3 1/4 borrows 1 from 6 as 4/4 but drops the original 1/4 (5 4/4 - 2 3/4); the borrowed 4/4 and the 1/4 together make 5/4.
n.2: 5 comes from borrowing 1 as 10/4 instead of 4/4 (5 11/4 - 2 3/4 = 3 8/4 = 5).

MA.q: A patient drinks 1 1/2 cups of water, 2 2/3 cups of tea and 3/4 cup of juice. What is the total intake in cups?

n.0: 3 2/3 adds the numerators and the denominators of the fractions: (1 + 2 + 3)/(2 + 3 + 4) = 6/9.
n.1: 3 11/12 drops the 1 whole carried from 23/12.
n.3: 4 3/4 renames 2/3 as 6/12 instead of 8/12, giving 3 21/12.

MA.q: Four patients' meal trays were checked after lunch. Ana ate 5/8 of her meal, Ben ate 0.63 of his, Cal ate 7/11 of his and Dev ate 0.6 of his. Who ate the greatest portion?
MA.w: Convert to decimals: Ana 5/8 = 0.625, Ben 0.630, Cal 7/11 = 0.6363..., Dev 0.600. The greatest is 0.636..., so Cal ate the most.

n.1: 0.6 = 0.600, the least of the four portions.
n.2: 0.63 = 0.630 is less than 7/11 = 0.636...; divide 7 by 11 to at least three places before comparing.

MA.q: A delivery van can safely carry a load of no more than 1.5 tons. Each crate of medical supplies weighs 140 pounds. What is the greatest number of crates the van can carry on one trip?

n.0: This reads 1.5 tons as 1 ton 500 pounds (2,500 lb); 0.5 ton = 1,000 lb.
n.2: 3,000 ÷ 140 = 21.4, and 22 crates weigh 3,080 lb, which is over the limit, so round down.
n.3: This uses 1,000 pounds per ton; 1 ton = 2,000 lb.

MA.q: A clinic thermometer shows a patient's temperature as 100.4 °F. The student nurse charting it needs the value in degrees Celsius. Which value is correct?

n.0: This rounds 5/9 to 0.55 before multiplying (68.4 x 0.55 = 37.6); 5/9 is 0.555..., so round only at the end.
n.1: This divides 68.4 by 2 instead of by 1.8 (dividing by 1.8 is the same as multiplying by 5/9).
n.3: This multiplies by 5/9 first and subtracts 32 afterward (100.4 x 5/9 = 55.8; 55.8 - 32 = 23.8); subtract 32 first.

MA.q: Which expression is NOT equal to 24 × 15?
MA.w: 24 × 15 = 360. The distributive property needs 24 to multiply BOTH parts of 10 + 5: 24 × 10 + 24 × 5 = 360. 24 × 10 + 5 = 245.

n.0: 24 × 10 + 24 × 5 = 240 + 120 = 360, a correct use of the distributive property.
n.3: 12 × 30 = 360: halving one factor and doubling the other keeps the product.

MA.q: A clinic reports that 0.6% of its scheduled appointments last month were canceled by the clinic. Which fraction, in lowest terms, is equivalent to 0.6%?
MA.w: Divide the percent by 100: 0.6% = 0.006 = 6/1,000. Divide both terms by 2: 3/500.

n.0: 3/5 = 0.6, which treats 0.6% as the decimal 0.6 (that is 60%).
n.1: 3/50 = 0.06, which is 6%. The decimal point was moved only 1 place left.
n.3: 3/5,000 = 0.0006, which is 0.06%. The decimal point was moved 3 places left instead of 2.

MA.q: A nurse measures a healing incision as 3 5/8 inches long and must record the length as a decimal in the electronic chart. Which decimal should be recorded?
MA.w: Convert the fraction part: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. Add the whole number: 3 + 0.625 = 3.625.

n.0: 0.375 is the decimal for 3/8, not 5/8.
n.1: This writes the digits 5 and 8 after the decimal point instead of dividing 5 by 8.
n.2: This divides 8 by 5 (1.6) instead of 5 by 8, then adds 3.

MA.q: A dietitian records the fraction of a daily sodium limit in four meals as 4/9, 0.449, 7/16 and 0.44. Which value is the least?
MA.w: Convert to decimals: 4/9 = 0.4444..., 0.449 = 0.4490, 7/16 = 0.4375 and 0.44 = 0.4400. Comparing place by place, 0.4375 is the least, so 7/16 is the least.

n.1: 0.449 = 0.4490 is the greatest of the four values.
n.2: 4/9 = 0.444..., which is greater than both 0.44 and 0.4375.
n.3: 0.44 = 0.4400 has 4 hundredths; 7/16 = 0.4375 has only 3, so 0.44 is greater.

MA.q: A patient's hospital bill is $1,350. The patient first pays a $250 deductible. The insurance plan then pays 80% of the remaining amount, and the patient pays the other 20%. How much does the patient pay in total?
MA.w: Remaining after the deductible: 1,350 - 250 = $1,100. Patient's share: 0.20 × 1,100 = $220. Total paid by the patient: 250 + 220 = $470.

n.0: This takes 20% of the full $1,350 and ignores the deductible.
n.1: This is the patient's 20% share of the $1,100 but leaves out the $250 deductible.
n.3: This takes 20% of the full $1,350 ($270) instead of 20% of the $1,100 left after the deductible, then adds $250.

MA.q: How many milligrams are in 0.004 kg?

n.0: This uses 100 mg per gram for the second step; 1 g = 1,000 mg.
n.2: 4 is the mass in grams; one more × 1,000 step is needed to reach milligrams.
n.3: This moves the decimal point one place too far (× 10,000,000).

MA.q: Which amount is the greatest?
MA.w: Put all in milligrams: 0.6 g = 600 mg; 550 mg; 650,000 mcg ÷ 1,000 = 650 mg; 0.0007 kg × 1,000,000 = 700 mg. 0.0007 kg is greatest.

n.0: 650,000 mcg = 650 mg; the large number reflects the tiny unit, and 650 mg is less than 700 mg.
n.2: 550 mg is less than 600, 650 and 700 mg.
n.3: 0.6 g = 600 mg, which is less than 700 mg.

MA.q: Which package of the same brand of oatmeal has the lowest price per ounce? (1 pound = 16 ounces)

n.1: $11.20 ÷ 32 ounces = $0.35 per ounce. Two pounds is 32 ounces, and $0.35 is still higher than $0.34.
n.2: $5.76 ÷ 16 ounces = $0.36 per ounce, higher than $0.34.
n.3: $4.44 ÷ 12 = $0.37 per ounce, the highest of the four.

MA.q: Write 6 4/10 as an improper fraction in lowest terms.

n.1: 64/10 has the right value, but 64 and 10 still share a factor of 2, so it is not in lowest terms.
n.2: 34/5 simplifies 4/10 to 2/5 but then adds the old numerator 4 instead of 2 (6 × 5 + 4).
n.3: 34/10 multiplies the whole number by the numerator and adds the denominator (6 × 4 + 10).

MA.q: A pharmacy technician has dispensed 3/8 of the tablets in a full stock bottle. Which percentage of the tablets in the bottle has been dispensed?
MA.w: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. Multiply by 100 (move the decimal point 2 places right): 0.375 = 37.5%.

n.1: This attaches a percent sign to the decimal 0.375 without multiplying by 100.
n.2: This moves the decimal point only 1 place right; 0.375 becomes 37.5%, not 3.75%.
n.3: This divides the denominator by the numerator (8 ÷ 3 = 2.667), which converts 8/3, not 3/8.

MA.q: Three coworkers split a $47.83 lunch bill equally. Each person's share is rounded up to the next cent so that the bill is fully covered. How much does each person pay?
MA.w: $47.83 ÷ 3 = $15.9433... Rounding up to the next cent gives $15.95. Check: 3 × $15.95 = $47.85, which covers the bill.

n.0: $16.00 rounds up to the next dollar, not the next cent.
n.2: $15.90 rounds down to the nearest ten cents and leaves the bill short.
n.3: $15.94 is ordinary rounding; 3 × $15.94 = $47.82, which is 1 cent short.

MA.q: A lab balance displays the mass of a sample as 47.0652 grams. The lab report requires masses rounded to the nearest hundredth of a gram. What mass should be reported?
MA.w: The hundredths digit is 6. The digit to its right (thousandths) is 5, so round up: 47.0652 → 47.07 g.

n.0: 47.065 g rounds to the nearest thousandth.
n.2: 47.1 g rounds to the nearest tenth, not the nearest hundredth.
n.3: 47.06 g truncates; the next digit is 5, so the hundredths digit rounds up.

MA.q: A scuba diver is 42 feet below the surface (-42 ft). She swims to a depth of 17 feet below the surface (-17 ft). Which describes the change in her position?
MA.w: Change = final - initial = -17 - (-42) = -17 + 42 = 25. A positive change means she rose 25 feet.

n.0: 59 adds the depths, and the direction is also wrong; -17 is closer to the surface.
n.1: The change is positive (-17 is above -42), so she moved up, not down.
n.2: 59 adds the two depths (42 + 17) instead of finding the difference.

MA.q: A patient is prescribed 1 tablespoon of cough syrup three times a day for 5 days. The pharmacy needs the total volume in milliliters. How many milliliters of cough syrup will the patient take over the full 5 days?
MA.w: 1 tbsp = 15 mL. Per day: 3 × 15 = 45 mL. For 5 days: 45 × 5 = 225 mL.

n.0: This uses 10 mL per tablespoon (2 teaspoons); 1 tbsp = 3 tsp = 15 mL.
n.2: This is one day's amount (3 × 15 mL); the course lasts 5 days.
n.3: This uses 5 mL, the volume of a teaspoon; 1 tbsp = 15 mL.

MA.w: Move both points 1 place right so the divisor is whole: 0.72 ÷ 9 = 0.08. Check: 0.08 × 0.9 = 0.072.

n.0: 0.8 moves the dividend's point 2 places while the divisor's moved 1.
n.1: 0.008 moves the divisor's point but not the dividend's (0.072 ÷ 9).
n.2: 8 divides 72 by 9 and loses track of the decimal point altogether.

MA.q: Which Roman numeral is written in standard form?
MA.w: XLV = 40 + 5 = 45, using the standard pair XL.

n.1: V is never subtracted; 45 is written XLV.
n.2: Only one I may be subtracted at a time; 8 is written VIII.
n.3: L never repeats; 100 is written C.

MA.q: A provider orders 0.375 gram of a medication to be given once daily. The pharmacy stocks the drug as tablets labeled in milligrams. How many milligrams of the drug does the daily order call for?
MA.w: Grams to milligrams is three steps down the metric ladder, so multiply by 1,000 (move the decimal point three places right): 0.375 × 1,000 = 375 mg.

n.0: This moves the decimal point four places instead of three.
n.1: This multiplies by 100, as if 1 gram were 100 milligrams; 1 g = 1,000 mg.
n.2: This divides by 1,000. Changing grams to the smaller unit, milligrams, means multiplying by 1,000.

MA.q: A patient may not eat for 8 hours before a procedure at 0730. What is the latest military time the patient may eat?
MA.w: Count back 8 hours from 0730: 7 h 30 min back reaches 0000, and 30 more minutes reaches 2330 the evening before.

n.0: This adds 12 hours instead of 24 before subtracting (1930 - 0800 = 1130).
n.1: This subtracts 7 h 30 min from 8 h and writes the 30-minute difference as a time.
n.3: This adds 8 hours to 0730 instead of counting back.

MA.q: A pancake recipe uses 1 1/2 cups of flour and 3/4 cup of milk. Kim has 2 cups of milk and wants to use all of it, keeping the same ratio of flour to milk. How many cups of flour does she need?
MA.w: Flour/milk: 1.5/0.75 = x/2. The recipe uses 2 cups of flour per cup of milk (1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2), so 2 × 2 = 4 cups of flour.

n.0: This sets up the ratio upside down, multiplying 2 by 3/4 and dividing by 1 1/2.
n.2: This multiplies 2 by 1 1/2 as if the 1 1/2 cups of flour went with 1 cup of milk.
n.3: This adds the extra 1 1/4 cups of milk to the flour instead of scaling.

MA.q: A pharmacy has a 10-pound tub of ointment base and uses 3 2/3 pounds. How many pounds remain?
MA.w: Borrow 1 whole from the 10 as 3/3: 10 = 9 3/3. Then 9 3/3 - 3 2/3 = 6 1/3 pounds. Check: 6 1/3 + 3 2/3 = 9 3/3 = 10.

n.0: 6 2/3 copies the 2/3 from the amount used instead of subtracting it from 3/3.
n.1: 7 1/3 finds 1 - 2/3 = 1/3 but does not take that 1 whole away from the 10.
n.2: 7 2/3 subtracts only the 3 whole pounds and keeps the 2/3 as part of what remains.

MA.q: A patient's fluid goal for the day is 2 1/4 liters. She has taken in 1 5/6 liters. How many more liters does she need to reach the goal?

n.1: 4 1/12 adds the goal and the intake; "how many more" needs a subtraction.
n.2: 1 5/12 adds the borrowed 12/12 to the fraction but does not take 1 from the 2.
n.3: 1 7/12 subtracts the smaller fraction from the larger (10/12 - 3/12) instead of borrowing.

MA.q: A home oral rehydration recipe calls for 6 level teaspoons of sugar per liter of clean water. A parent is making 1.5 liters of the solution but has a tablespoon measure and no teaspoon. How many tablespoons of sugar are needed?
MA.w: Teaspoons needed = 6 × 1.5 = 9 tsp. Since 1 tbsp = 3 tsp, 9 ÷ 3 = 3 tbsp.

n.0: 9 is the number of teaspoons (6 × 1.5); divide by 3 to change teaspoons to tablespoons.
n.1: This multiplies the 9 teaspoons by 3 instead of dividing.
n.3: This uses 2 teaspoons per tablespoon; 1 tbsp = 3 tsp.

MA.q: A regional hospital system reported serving 248,513 patients last year. What is this number rounded to the nearest ten thousand?
MA.w: The ten-thousands digit is 4 (in 248,513). The digit to its right is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up: 250,000.

n.0: 200,000 is rounded to the nearest hundred thousand.
n.1: 249,000 is rounded to the nearest thousand.
n.3: 240,000 truncates; the thousands digit 8 means rounding up.

MA.q: A disinfectant is mixed using 1 part concentrate to 19 parts water. What percent of the mixture is concentrate? Round to the nearest tenth.
MA.w: Total parts: 1 + 19 = 20. Concentrate: 1/20 = 0.05 = 5.0%.

n.0: This is the percent of the mixture that is water (19/20).
n.1: This divides 1 by 19, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole mixture.
n.3: This moves the decimal point only one place. 0.05 = 5.0%.

MA.q: Which number is three hundred six and twelve thousandths?
MA.w: Three hundred six = 306. Twelve thousandths must end in the thousandths place (third place): 0.012. Together: 306.012.

n.0: 306.0012 is twelve ten-thousandths, one place too far right.
n.1: 36.012 drops the zero in the tens place of three hundred six.
n.3: 306.12 is twelve hundredths, not twelve thousandths.

MA.q: A patient drank 2/3 cup of juice at breakfast and 3/4 cup of juice at lunch. How many cups of juice did the patient drink in all?
MA.w: Use the LCD of 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Add the numerators: 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12 cups.

n.0: 1/2 is the product 2/3 × 3/4; the question asks for a total, so add.
n.1: 5/7 adds the numerators (2 + 3) and the denominators (3 + 4); denominators are not added together.
n.3: 1 1/12 = 13/12. It rewrites 2/3 as 4/12; the numerator must be multiplied by 4, giving 8/12.

MA.q: Write 49 in Roman numerals.
MA.w: 49 = 40 + 9 = XL + IX = XLIX. I may be subtracted only from V or X, so 49 is not IL.

n.1: IL is not standard: I is subtracted only from V or X, never from L.
n.3: X may not repeat four times; 40 is written XL.

MA.q: Evaluate 4 + 12 × 4 - 8 ÷ 2.
MA.w: Multiply and divide first: 12 × 4 = 48 and 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Then add and subtract left to right: 4 + 48 - 4 = 48.

n.0: 22 divides the whole sum by 2: (4 + 48 - 8) ÷ 2.
n.2: 28 works strictly left to right, as a basic calculator does: ((4 + 12) × 4 - 8) ÷ 2.
n.3: -20 subtracts 4 - 8 before multiplying: 4 + 12 × (-4) ÷ 2.

MA.q: A child weighs 33 lb. The dose ordered is 0.5 mg per kilogram. How many micrograms are in the dose?

n.0: This converts 7.5 mg with a factor of 100; 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.
n.1: This uses 33 lb as if it were kilograms (33 × 0.5 = 16.5 mg).
n.3: This multiplies 33 by 2.2 (72.6 kg) instead of dividing.

MA.q: A 1,000 mL IV bag infuses at 125 mL per hour for 3.5 hours, then at 75 mL per hour for 2.5 hours. How many milliliters remain in the bag? Enter the number only.

tr.250: Used 125 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.550: Used 75 mL per hour for all 6 hours.
tr.625: Gave the volume infused instead of the volume remaining.

MA.w: First rate: 3.5 × 125 = 437.5 mL. Second rate: 2.5 × 75 = 187.5 mL. Infused: 437.5 + 187.5 = 625 mL. Remaining: 1,000 - 625 = 375 mL.

MA.q: A pediatric dose of a medication is 2/5 of the adult dose. The adult dose is 37 1/2 mg. What is the pediatric dose?
MA.w: Write the adult dose as an improper fraction: 37 1/2 = 75/2. Multiply: 2/5 × 75/2 = 150/10 = 15 mg.

n.1: 22 1/2 mg is 3/5 of the adult dose (the part not given), not 2/5.
n.2: 15 3/10 multiplies only the whole number (2/5 × 37 = 14 4/5) and then adds the 1/2 unchanged.
n.3: 93 3/4 divides 37 1/2 by 2/5 instead of taking 2/5 of it.

MA.q: A clinic saw 240 patients last week. 35% were children, and 1/4 of the children needed a vaccine. How many children needed a vaccine?
MA.w: Children: 0.35 × 240 = 84. Needing a vaccine: 1/4 × 84 = 21.

n.0: 63 is the number of children who did not need a vaccine (84 - 21).
n.2: 60 takes 1/4 of all 240 patients instead of 1/4 of the 84 children.
n.3: 84 is the number of children, one step short of the answer.

MA.q: A clinic scheduled 80 appointments on Tuesday, and 12 patients did not show up. What percent of the scheduled appointments were kept?
MA.w: Appointments kept: 80 - 12 = 68. Percent kept = 68 ÷ 80 × 100 = 85%.

n.0: This subtracts 12 ÷ 68 from 100%. The whole is the 80 scheduled appointments.
n.1: This is the no-show rate, 12 ÷ 80, not the percent of appointments kept.
n.2: This divides 12 by 68, using the kept appointments as the whole instead of all 80 scheduled.

MA.w: Write 30 as 30.000. Borrowing gives 2 tens, 9 ones, 9 tenths, 9 hundredths and 10 thousandths: 10 - 7 = 3, 9 - 5 = 4, 9 - 4 = 5, 9 - 2 = 7, 2 - 1 = 1. Answer 17.543. Check: 17.543 + 12.457 = 30.

n.0: 18.653 turns each zero into 10 without reducing it to 9 after lending.
n.1: 18.457 subtracts only the whole numbers (30 - 12) and keeps the .457.
n.3: 22.457 takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing.

MA.q: Between 8 a.m. and noon, a patient's temperature rose from 37.2 °C to 38.7 °C. The family asks how much the temperature went up in Fahrenheit terms. By how many degrees Fahrenheit did the temperature rise?

n.1: 1.5 is the rise in degrees Celsius; each Celsius degree equals 9/5 Fahrenheit degrees.
n.2: This adds 32 to the change. The 32 shifts the starting point of the scale, so it cancels out of a difference.
n.3: This multiplies the 1.5 °C change by 5/9 instead of 9/5.

AP.q: Which statement correctly describes the pleural membranes and the fluid between them?
o: Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid lowers alveolar surface tension
Visceral pleura covers each lung and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
Parietal pleura covers each lung and visceral pleura lines the thoracic wall; the fluid reduces friction
AP.w: Visceral pleura covers the lung surface and parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall. Pleural fluid between them reduces friction and holds the lungs against the chest wall so they expand with it.

n.0: Both parts are wrong: visceral pleura is the layer on the lung, and lowering alveolar surface tension is the role of surfactant, not pleural fluid.
n.1: The membranes are named correctly, but lowering alveolar surface tension is the job of surfactant inside the alveoli; pleural fluid lies outside the lung and reduces friction.
n.3: The layers are reversed: visceral means on the organ (the lung), parietal means on the cavity wall.

AP.q: Which statement correctly describes how materials pass between mother and fetus at the placenta?
o: Gases and nutrients cross; the two bloodstreams stay apart
Maternal and fetal blood mix, so gases equalize directly
Nutrients cross, but the fetus gets its O2 from amniotic fluid
Gases cross, but nutrients reach the fetus in amniotic fluid
AP.w: At the placenta, oxygen, nutrients, wastes and some antibodies (IgG) diffuse between maternal and fetal blood across thin barriers. The two bloodstreams do not mix. The placenta also acts as an endocrine organ.

n.1: Maternal and fetal blood do not mix; exchange happens across the barrier between them.
n.2: Oxygen reaches the fetus from maternal blood across the placenta, not from the amniotic fluid.
n.3: Nutrients cross at the placenta into fetal blood; amniotic fluid cushions the fetus rather than feeding it.

AP.q: A biopsy of the sciatic nerve, which is part of the peripheral nervous system, shows myelinated axons. Which cells produced the myelin sheath around these axons?
AP.w: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is made by Schwann cells. In the central nervous system, oligodendrocytes make it.

n.0: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS, not in peripheral nerves such as the sciatic nerve.
n.2: Satellite cells are PNS glia that surround cell bodies in ganglia; Schwann cells form PNS myelin.
n.3: Astrocytes are CNS glia that support neurons and help form the blood-brain barrier; they do not make myelin.

AP.q: A student argues that a single cardiac muscle cell taken from the heart should be classified at the tissue level. Which statement best explains why this classification is incorrect?
o: A muscle cell belongs at the chemical level because it is made of proteins
A tissue is a group of similar cells working together, and this is a single cell
A tissue requires an extracellular matrix of fibers, which one muscle cell lacks
A tissue must be supplied by blood vessels, and a single muscle cell has none
AP.w: A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together. One cell on its own, even a highly specialized one, is classified at the cellular level.

n.0: Proteins are at the chemical level, but a whole living cell built from them is at the cellular level.
n.2: An abundant extracellular matrix is a feature of connective tissue. Epithelial and muscle tissues have very little matrix between their cells, yet they are still tissues.
n.3: Epithelium is a tissue but is avascular, so blood vessels are not what makes something a tissue.

AP.q: In the nine-region scheme of the abdomen, three regions run down the midline. Which region lies directly inferior to the umbilical region?
AP.w: The middle column of the nine regions runs epigastric (top), umbilical (middle), hypogastric or pubic (bottom). The hypogastric region lies directly below the umbilical region.

n.0: The right lumbar region lies lateral to the umbilical region, in the middle row.
n.2: The epigastric region lies directly superior to the umbilical region, not inferior to it.
n.3: The left iliac (inguinal) region is in the bottom row but lateral, not directly below the umbilical region.

AP.q: A tissue sample taken just beneath the epidermis contains blood vessels, nerve endings, hair follicles and a dense mesh of collagen and elastin fibers. Which layer and tissue type does it show?
o: Smooth muscle tissue of the dermis
AP.w: The dermis lies beneath the epidermis and is connective tissue: areolar in the papillary layer and dense irregular in the reticular layer, rich in collagen (strength) and elastin (stretch), with vessels, nerves, follicles and glands.

n.0: The dermis does contain tiny arrector pili muscles, but its main tissue is connective tissue, not smooth muscle.
n.2: The epidermis is avascular stratified squamous epithelium; it has no blood vessels or collagen mesh.
n.3: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat with areolar tissue, not a dense collagen and elastin mesh.

AP.q: An autoimmune process destroys a patient's adrenal cortex but spares the adrenal medulla. Which hormone deficiencies, and which effect, would be expected?
o: Low epinephrine and norepinephrine; a weaker fight-or-flight response
Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood glucose from gluconeogenesis
Low cortisol and aldosterone; low blood pressure from Na⁺ loss
Low cortisol and aldosterone; high blood pressure from Na⁺ retention
AP.w: Two steps: the adrenal cortex makes cortisol and aldosterone, so both fall (Addison's disease). Without aldosterone the kidneys lose Na⁺ and the water that follows it, so blood volume and blood pressure fall.

n.0: Epinephrine and norepinephrine come from the adrenal medulla, which is spared.
n.1: The deficiencies are right, but cortisol raises blood glucose by gluconeogenesis, so losing it tends to lower glucose rather than raise it.
n.3: The deficiencies are right, but aldosterone causes Na⁺ retention, so its loss leads to Na⁺ loss and lower blood pressure.

AP.q: About 99% of the filtrate formed each day is returned to the blood. Which part of the nephron reabsorbs the largest share of the filtered water and sodium?
o: Ascending limb of the nephron loop
AP.w: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs the most: normally all of the glucose and amino acids and about 65% of the sodium and water, plus bicarbonate.

n.0: The collecting duct fine-tunes water reabsorption under ADH, but it handles a much smaller share than the PCT.
n.1: The ascending limb pumps out sodium and chloride but is impermeable to water.
n.3: The DCT fine-tunes sodium, potassium and calcium under hormones; it is not the main site of bulk reabsorption.

AP.q: In anatomical position, which pairing correctly describes where the radius lies in the forearm and where the tibia lies in the leg?
AP.w: In anatomical position (palms forward) the radius is on the lateral, thumb side of the forearm and the ulna is medial. In the leg the large, weight-bearing tibia is medial and the thin fibula is lateral.

n.0: The tibia is medial; the lateral leg bone is the fibula.
n.2: The radius is lateral; the medial forearm bone is the ulna.
n.3: Both are reversed: the ulna is the medial forearm bone and the fibula is the lateral leg bone.

AP.q: After pancreatic lipase splits dietary fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides, intestinal cells repackage them for absorption. Into which vessels do these fats first pass, and in what form?
o: Villus blood capillaries, as free fatty acids
Lacteals in the villi, as monosaccharides
The hepatic portal vein, as triglycerides
Lacteals in the villi, as chylomicrons
AP.w: Absorptive cells package digested fats into chylomicrons, which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals, the lymphatic capillaries of the villi.

n.0: Sugars and amino acids enter blood capillaries; fats enter the lymph through lacteals.
n.1: Lacteals are the right vessels, but monosaccharides are sugars and are absorbed into blood capillaries.
n.2: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed sugars and amino acids to the liver, not chylomicrons.

AP.q: A patient is asked to rise up onto the toes. Which movement occurs at the ankle, and which muscles act as the prime movers?
o: Plantar flexion by the tibialis anterior
Dorsiflexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
Plantar flexion by the gastrocnemius and soleus
AP.w: Step 1: rising onto the toes points the foot downward, which is plantar flexion. Step 2: the prime movers of plantar flexion are the gastrocnemius and soleus, acting through the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.

n.0: The tibialis anterior produces dorsiflexion, not plantar flexion.
n.1: The gastrocnemius and soleus plantar flex the ankle; dorsiflexion is the action of the tibialis anterior.
n.2: Dorsiflexion lifts the toes toward the shin, the opposite of rising onto the toes.

AP.q: After a stroke, Mr. Okafor understands questions but struggles to produce fluent speech. Damage to which area, in which lobe, best explains this?
o: Broca's area in the frontal lobe
Broca's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe
Wernicke's area in the frontal lobe
AP.w: Two steps: trouble producing speech with comprehension intact points to Broca's area (speech production), and Broca's area lies in the frontal lobe, usually on the left.

n.1: Broca's area is the right area, but it lies in the frontal lobe, not the temporal lobe.
n.2: Wernicke's area handles language comprehension, which is intact here.
n.3: Wernicke's area handles comprehension and lies in the temporal lobe, so both parts are wrong.

AP.q: During a long run on a hot day, a runner's sweat glands release sweat, and its evaporation cools the skin. In this feedback loop, which role do the sweat glands play?
AP.w: An effector is the muscle or gland that produces the response. The sweat glands carry out the cooling response directed by the control center (the hypothalamus).

n.0: The control center for body temperature is the hypothalamus in the brain, which directs the sweat glands.
n.1: Receptors are the temperature sensors that detect the rise; the sweat glands respond to the change.
n.3: The set point is the target value (normal body temperature), not a structure.

AP.q: A histology student is comparing the four basic tissue types. Which feature distinguishes connective tissue from epithelial, muscle and nervous tissue?
o: Cells that generate and conduct electrical impulses
Cells scattered within an extracellular matrix of fibers
Cells joined tightly together with an exposed free surface
Cells that shorten when stimulated to produce movement
AP.w: Connective tissue cells are scattered within an extracellular matrix made of ground substance and fibers (collagen, elastic, reticular). In blood, the matrix is fluid plasma.

n.0: Generating and conducting impulses describes the neurons of nervous tissue.
n.2: Tightly joined cells with a free (apical) surface describe epithelial tissue.
n.3: Contractility describes muscle tissue.

AP.q: In a fetus, the umbilical vein carries blood from the placenta to the fetus. Based on how veins are defined, which statement is correct?
o: It carries deoxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart
It carries oxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
It carries deoxygenated blood away from the fetal heart
AP.w: Step 1: a vein carries blood toward the heart. Step 2: blood leaving the placenta has picked up oxygen, so the umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood toward the fetal heart (the umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away).

n.0: Blood coming from the placenta has just been oxygenated there.
n.2: Carrying blood away from the heart would make it an artery.
n.3: This describes the umbilical arteries, which return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.

AP.q: A red blood cell leaves the left ventricle, travels to a capillary in the big toe and eventually returns to the left ventricle. Which capillary beds does it pass through, and in what order?
o: Two beds: the toe, then the pulmonary capillaries
Three beds: the toe, the coronary bed, then the lungs
Two beds: the pulmonary capillaries, then the toe
One bed: the systemic capillaries in the toe
AP.w: Step 1: from the left ventricle the cell goes through systemic arteries to the toe capillaries, then back by veins to the right atrium. Step 2: the right ventricle sends it to the pulmonary capillaries, and the pulmonary veins return it to the left atrium and left ventricle. Two beds, systemic first.

n.1: The coronary bed is a separate branch of the systemic circuit, not a stop on the route to and from the toe.
n.2: Leaving the left ventricle, it enters the systemic circuit first; the lungs come after the right ventricle.
n.3: To get back to the left ventricle it must also pass through the lungs, a second capillary bed.

AP.q: A gallstone blocks the bile duct before it joins the pancreatic duct, so bile cannot reach the duodenum. Which digestive process in the small intestine is most directly impaired?
o: Splitting of maltose by brush-border maltase
Absorption of glucose into villus capillaries
AP.w: Bile salts emulsify fat. If bile cannot reach the duodenum, fat stays in large droplets, so fat digestion by lipase and its absorption suffer.

n.0: Maltase sits on the microvilli of the small intestine and splits maltose without any help from bile.
n.2: Trypsin comes from the pancreas; the block is above the pancreatic duct, so pancreatic juice still flows.
n.3: Glucose is absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi, a process that does not depend on bile.

AP.q: A cell infected with a virus secretes proteins that diffuse to nearby cells and help those cells resist infection by the virus. Which innate defense does this describe?
AP.w: Interferons are made by virus-infected cells and protect neighboring cells, an innate second-line defense.

n.0: Antibodies come from plasma cells in the adaptive response, not from the infected cell itself.
n.2: Histamine from mast cells drives inflammation; it does not help neighboring cells resist a virus.
n.3: Complement proteins circulate in plasma, lyse microbes and enhance phagocytosis; infected cells do not secrete them to protect their neighbors.

AP.q: Directional terms in anatomy are defined relative to anatomical position. Which description matches anatomical position?
o: Lying face up, arms at the sides, palms facing up, feet pointing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms raised, palms facing forward
Standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing the thighs
AP.w: In anatomical position the body is upright and facing forward, feet flat and pointing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward (anterior) with the thumbs pointing away from the body.

n.0: Lying face up is the supine position. Anatomical position is upright.
n.2: The arms hang at the sides in anatomical position; they are not raised.
n.3: Palms facing the thighs is a relaxed standing posture. In anatomical position the palms face forward.

AP.q: Fingerprint ridges come from the dermal layer just beneath the epidermis, which also holds the receptors for light touch. Which layer is this?
AP.w: The dermis has two layers. The thin, superficial papillary layer forms the dermal papillae that create fingerprint ridges and holds Meissner corpuscles for light touch. The deeper reticular layer is dense collagen and elastin with hair follicles, glands and Pacinian corpuscles.

n.1: The stratum basale is the deepest layer of the epidermis, not a layer of the dermis.
n.2: The hypodermis lies beneath the dermis and is mostly fat; it is not part of the dermis.
n.3: The reticular layer is the deeper, thicker part of the dermis; it does not form the ridges under the epidermis.

AP.q: A patient receives a large volume of intravenous fluid, and the increased blood volume stretches the walls of the heart's atria. Which response helps return blood volume toward normal?
o: ADH is released, adding aquaporins to collecting ducts
Renin is released, increasing angiotensin II
ANP is released, increasing sodium and water excretion
ANP is released, increasing sodium reabsorption
AP.w: Stretched atria release atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which makes the kidneys lose more sodium and water, lowering blood volume and blood pressure: the opposite of RAAS.

n.0: ADH increases water reabsorption, which would raise blood volume further.
n.1: Renin and angiotensin II raise blood volume and pressure, which would worsen the overload.
n.3: ANP is the right hormone, but it increases sodium excretion; sodium reabsorption is aldosterone's effect.

AP.q: In the classification of bones by shape, to which category does the patella (kneecap) belong?
AP.w: Sesamoid bones form within tendons, and the patella is the classic example. Short bones are cube-like (carpals, tarsals), flat bones are thin (cranial bones, sternum, ribs, scapulae) and irregular bones include the vertebrae.

n.0: Irregular bones, such as the vertebrae, have complex shapes and do not develop within tendons.
n.1: Flat bones are thin and often curved, such as the cranial bones, sternum, ribs and scapulae.
n.3: Short bones are roughly cube-shaped, such as the carpals and tarsals, and do not form inside tendons.

AP.q: In the thyroid axis, rising blood levels of T3 and T4 reduce the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. What type of control is this?
AP.w: The end product (T3 and T4) switches off the signals that produced it, reversing the change. That is negative feedback, the way most hormone levels are controlled.

n.1: Positive feedback amplifies a change until an end event, as oxytocin does in labor; here the change is being reversed.
n.2: The signals in this loop travel as hormones in the blood, not along nerves.
n.3: Antagonistic control means two hormones with opposite effects, such as insulin and glucagon; this is one hormone suppressing its own signals.

AP.q: A diagram shows a patient facing the viewer, and an instructor points to the lower abdominal quadrant on the viewer's left side. Which organ is located in that quadrant?
AP.w: Two steps: a patient facing the viewer has their right side on the viewer's left, so the instructor is pointing to the patient's right lower quadrant (RLQ), which contains the appendix and cecum.

n.0: The spleen is in the left upper quadrant, not a lower quadrant.
n.2: The gallbladder is in the right upper quadrant, under the liver, not a lower quadrant.
n.3: The sigmoid colon is in the left lower quadrant. That is the patient's left, which appears on the viewer's right.

AP.q: In an alveolus, which cell type secretes surfactant, and what does surfactant do?
o: Type II alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type I alveolar cells; it lowers surface tension so alveoli resist collapse
Type II alveolar cells; it raises surface tension so alveoli recoil on expiration
Alveolar macrophages; it coats inhaled dust so the dust can be digested
AP.w: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactant, which lowers the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli so they do not collapse at the end of each breath.

n.1: The effect is right but the cell is wrong: type I cells are thin squamous cells specialized for gas exchange.
n.2: The cell is right but the effect is reversed: surfactant decreases surface tension.
n.3: Alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf particles; they do not make surfactant.

AP.q: Which glial cells of the central nervous system wrap brain capillaries with their processes and help form the blood-brain barrier?
AP.w: Astrocytes are star-shaped CNS glia that support neurons and, with their processes on brain capillaries, help form the blood-brain barrier.

n.0: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and help make cerebrospinal fluid.
n.1: Microglia are the phagocytes of the CNS; they do not form the blood-brain barrier.
n.2: Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS.

AP.q: After the impulse passes through the AV bundle (bundle of His), which structures does it travel through next?
AP.w: Conduction runs SA node, AV node, AV bundle (bundle of His), right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum, then Purkinje fibers in the ventricular walls.

n.0: The AV node comes before the bundle of His; it delays the impulse so the ventricles can fill.
n.2: The Purkinje fibers come after the bundle branches; they spread the impulse through the ventricular myocardium.
n.3: The SA node starts each impulse in the wall of the right atrium, at the very beginning of the pathway.

AP.q: Counting the carpals, metacarpals and phalanges, how many bones form the skeleton of one adult hand, from the wrist to the fingertips?
AP.w: 8 carpals + 5 metacarpals + 14 phalanges = 27. The thumb has 2 phalanges and each of the other four fingers has 3, so the phalanges total 2 + (4 x 3) = 14.

n.0: This comes from giving the thumb 3 phalanges like the other fingers (8 + 5 + 15).
n.1: This comes from counting one phalanx per digit (8 + 5 + 5).
n.3: This comes from using 7 carpals, which is the number of tarsals in the foot (7 + 5 + 14).

AP.q: Shortly after Jamal eats a large pasta dinner, his blood glucose rises. Which hormone does his pancreas release in response, and from which cells?
AP.w: High blood glucose after a meal triggers the beta cells of the pancreatic islets to release insulin, which lowers glucose by moving it into cells and storing it as glycogen.

n.0: Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it is released when glucose is low, not after a meal.
n.2: Insulin is the right hormone, but it comes from beta cells; alpha cells make glucagon.
n.3: Glucagon raises blood glucose and is made by alpha cells, so both parts are wrong.

AP.q: Skeletal muscle fibers are wide cells, yet all their myofibrils contract almost at the same moment. What do the transverse (T) tubules do that makes this possible?
o: Carry the impulse deep into the fiber
Anchor thin filaments at each Z disc
AP.w: T-tubules are inward folds of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fiber, next to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so Ca²⁺ is released around every myofibril at once.

n.0: Calcium is stored in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, not in the T-tubules.
n.1: Acetylcholine is released by the motor neuron's axon terminal at the neuromuscular junction.
n.3: Thin filaments are anchored at the Z discs themselves; T-tubules conduct the impulse.

BI.q: A liver cell begins making albumin by copying the albumin gene into messenger RNA. Where does this step take place, and which enzyme carries it out?
o: In the nucleus, by DNA polymerase
At the ribosome, by RNA polymerase
In the nucleus, by RNA polymerase
BI.w: Copying DNA into mRNA is transcription. In eukaryotes it happens in the nucleus, where RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand and builds complementary mRNA.

n.0: DNA polymerase copies DNA into DNA during replication, not DNA into RNA.
n.1: Helicase unwinds DNA during replication; transcription happens in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm.
n.2: The ribosome is the site of translation, not transcription.

BI.q: At the end of mitosis, a plant root cell divides its cytoplasm differently from an animal cell. Which structure forms between the two new plant cells?
o: A nuclear envelope that splits the cell
A centriole pair that pulls the cell apart
A cleavage furrow that pinches inward
A cell plate that becomes a new wall
BI.w: In plant cells, cytokinesis builds a cell plate across the middle that develops into a new cell wall. Animal cells pinch in with a cleavage furrow.

n.0: Nuclear envelopes re-form around each set of chromosomes in telophase; they do not divide the cytoplasm.
n.1: Most plant cells lack centrioles, and centrioles organize the spindle rather than splitting the cytoplasm.
n.2: A cleavage furrow is how animal cells divide their cytoplasm; the rigid plant wall prevents pinching.

BI.q: A researcher isolates the fluid-filled interior (matrix) of mitochondria. Which stage of cellular respiration would be active in this fraction?
BI.w: The Krebs (citric acid) cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, releasing CO2 and loading NADH and FADH2.

n.0: The electron transport chain is built into the inner membrane (cristae), not the matrix fluid.
n.2: The Calvin cycle is part of photosynthesis in the chloroplast stroma.
n.3: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria.

BI.q: A cell has a membrane-bound nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall, but no chloroplasts. Of the following, which is the most likely source of this cell?
BI.w: Step 1: a nucleus and mitochondria mean the cell is eukaryotic, which rules out bacteria. Step 2: a cell wall without chloroplasts fits a fungus such as yeast, which has a chitin wall and cannot photosynthesize.

n.1: Bacteria have cell walls but are prokaryotes, so they have no nucleus or mitochondria.
n.2: A moss leaf cell has a wall and nucleus, but as a photosynthetic leaf cell it contains chloroplasts.
n.3: Human cells are eukaryotic with mitochondria, but animal cells have no cell wall.

BI.q: A student builds a model of one DNA nucleotide for a biology display. Which three components should the model include?
o: An amino group, a carboxyl group and an R group
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, deoxyribose and a nitrogenous base
Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group
BI.w: A nucleotide is a phosphate group + a 5-carbon sugar + a nitrogenous base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose.

n.0: An amino group, carboxyl group and R group are the parts of an amino acid, the monomer of proteins.
n.1: Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides; DNA uses deoxyribose.
n.3: Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate make up a phospholipid, not a nucleotide.

BI.q: In liver cells, the enzyme catalase greatly speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. How does catalase increase the reaction rate?
o: It increases the total energy the reaction releases.
It is consumed and becomes part of the products.
It shifts the equilibrium toward more products.
It lowers the activation energy of the reaction.
BI.w: Enzymes are biological catalysts: they lower activation energy, are not consumed, and do not change the overall energy released.

n.0: Enzymes do not change the overall energy change of the reaction, only the energy needed to start it.
n.1: Enzymes are not consumed; they are released unchanged and reused.
n.2: Enzymes do not change the equilibrium of a reaction; they help it reach equilibrium faster.

BI.q: How do ATP and ADP differ in structure?
o: ATP contains adenine; ADP contains guanine.
ATP has three phosphate groups; ADP has two.
ATP has two phosphate groups; ADP has three.
ATP contains ribose; ADP contains deoxyribose.
BI.w: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) has three phosphate groups. Removing one by hydrolysis gives ADP (adenosine diphosphate) + Pi and releases energy.

n.0: Both contain adenine; the A in ATP and ADP stands for adenosine.
n.2: The counts are reversed: tri- means three (ATP), di- means two (ADP).
n.3: Both contain ribose; deoxyribose is the sugar in DNA.

BI.q: Which of the following mutations in the coding region of a gene is most likely to change every amino acid after the mutation site?
o: A substitution that keeps the same amino acid
A substitution that changes one amino acid
BI.w: Step 1: codons are read in groups of three. Step 2: deleting one base (not a multiple of three) shifts the reading frame, so every downstream codon is misread: a frameshift.

n.0: Deleting three bases removes one codon (one amino acid) and keeps the reading frame intact downstream.
n.2: A silent substitution does not change the amino acid at all.
n.3: A missense substitution changes only one amino acid; the reading frame is unaffected.

BI.q: Two sisters with the same parents differ genetically partly because segments were exchanged between homologous chromosomes while their parents' gametes formed. When does this exchange take place?
BI.w: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) as tetrads and exchange segments.

n.0: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
n.1: Homologs are no longer paired in prophase II, so crossing over between them does not occur then.
n.2: Anaphase I is when homologs separate; the exchange had already happened in prophase I.

BI.q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which feature of phospholipid structure explains this arrangement?
o: Their tails are polar and are attracted to the surrounding water.
Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward.
Their three fatty acid tails make them dissolve in water.
Their nonpolar heads face water while polar tails face inward.
BI.w: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic (polar) phosphate head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acid tails. In water the heads face outward and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.

n.0: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so they avoid water.
n.2: Phospholipids have two fatty acid tails (triglycerides have three), and the tails repel water.
n.3: Polarity is reversed: the heads are polar and the tails are nonpolar.

BI.q: A father with type A blood (genotype IAi) and a mother with type B blood (genotype IBi) are expecting a child. Which blood types are possible for the child?
o: A and B, but not AB or O
A, B and AB, but not O
